chief_complaint: intense itching after hot showers, ruddy complexion, and burning toes
hpi_details: 56F presenting with aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, hematocrit 58%, and suppressed EPO level. JAK2 V617F mutation positive.
ideas: She thinks she has developed a severe allergy to the chemicals in her tap water along with poor circulation in her feet.
concerns: She is worried that the redness and burning mean she has an underlying autoimmune disease like lupus that will force her to quit her job.
expectations: She hopes for a prescription lotion or allergy pill that will calm the agonizing itching so she can take normal showers again.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Polycythemia Vera is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes therapeutic phlebotomy to keep hematocrit below 45%, low-dose aspirin for thrombosis prophylaxis, and cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea) for high-risk patients, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: intense itching after hot showers, ruddy complexion, and burning toes
Key HPI features: 56F presenting with aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, hematocrit 58%, and suppressed EPO level. JAK2 V617F mutation positive.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 36.8C, HR 78, BP 148/92, SpO2 97% on room air. Plethoric (ruddy) facial complexion, conjunctival injection, palpable splenomegaly (spleen tip 3-4cm below left costal margin), excoriations from scratching, erythema and warmth of the toes bilaterally. Bloods: Hemoglobin 19.8 g/dL, Hematocrit 58%, WBC 12,500/uL, Platelets 480,000/uL, serum erythropoietin (EPO) suppressed/low. JAK2 V617F mutation positive.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Polycythemia Vera.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Secondary polycythemia (from hypoxia/smoking) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Symptoms of stroke or clot (weakness, vision changes) — hyperviscosity raises thrombosis risk.
management_principles: Therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce hematocrit below 45% (target per CYTO-PV trial), removing 250-500mL per session and repeating as needed
Start low-dose aspirin 81mg daily for thrombosis prophylaxis unless contraindicated
Risk-stratify by age and thrombosis history: reserve cytoreductive therapy (Hydroxyurea 500-1000mg daily) for high-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombosis)
Confirm diagnosis with JAK2 V617F mutation testing and serum erythropoietin level; monitor CBC every 3 months
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

JAK2 V617F mutation positive.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 36.8C, HR 78, BP 148/92, SpO2 97% on room air. Plethoric (ruddy) facial complexion, conjunctival injection, palpable splenomegaly (spleen tip 3-4cm below left costal margin), excoriations from scratching, erythema and warmth of the toes bilaterally. reference_soap.assessment: Polycythemia Vera (PV) presenting with aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, and plethora secondary to a JAK2 V617F-driven myeloproliferative process with hyperviscosity risk.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce hematocrit to target <45%, removing 250-500mL initially and repeating as needed. 2. Start low-dose aspirin 81mg daily for thrombosis prophylaxis. 3. Risk-stratify: age 56 with no prior thrombosis places her in the lower-risk category — phlebotomy plus aspirin is primary therapy; reserve hydroxyurea for high-risk features. 4. Confirm JAK2 V617F mutation (already positive) and suppressed serum EPO to satisfy WHO diagnostic criteria; consider bone marrow biopsy if diagnosis remains uncertain. 5. Refer to hematology for ongoing CBC monitoring every 3 months and counseling on cardiovascular risk reduction and hydration.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Polycythemia Vera JAK2 Mutation
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for intense itching after hot showers, ruddy complexion, and burning toes
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for hematology_oncology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A JAK2-mutated myeloproliferative disorder causing overproduction of red blood cells, presenting with itching after hot water, a ruddy complexion, and burning pain in the extremities.
red_flags: Symptoms of stroke or clot (weakness, vision changes) — hyperviscosity raises thrombosis risk

must_ask.say: Does the itching happen specifically after hot showers?
Have people commented that your face looks unusually red or flushed?
Do your toes or fingers burn or feel painfully hot?
Any headaches, dizziness, or visual changes?
Do you smoke, or have any lung conditions?

history.answer: Doctor, I have been suffering from unbearable itching all over my body whenever I take a warm shower, and my face looks unusually flushed.
The itching started gradually about two to three months ago, but it has become much more intense over the past few weeks.
It happens almost every single time right after stepping out of a warm shower or bath, lasting for about thirty to forty-five minutes.
It itches all over my chest, back, arms, and legs, but I do not see any hives or skin rash except where I scratch.
It feels like an intense prickling and stinging sensation all over, easily an eight out of ten in severity right after bathing.
Each episode lasts around forty-five minutes before gradually fading, and the attacks have grown more severe over the past month.
Warm or hot water definitely triggers and worsens it. Taking quick, cool showers helps slightly, but nothing completely stops the itch.
Yes, my toes and the balls of my feet frequently feel uncomfortably hot, red, and burning, especially in the evening.
My coworkers and friends keep asking why my face looks so red and ruddy all the time, even when I am just resting.
I have felt a bit full rather quickly after eating lately, and there is a mild sensation of heaviness under my left ribs.
I have had a dull, full feeling in my head and occasional dizziness over the last couple of months.
No, I have not had any sudden weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, or changes in my vision.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or drenching night sweats.
My weight has been completely steady, though I have been feeling a little more tired than usual.
No, I have not had unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or bleeding from my gums.
No, my breathing is fine, and I do not have a chronic cough or chest pain.
No, I have never had this kind of severe post-shower itching or burning feet in my life.
I tried using over-the-counter anti-itch creams and oral allergy pills, but they did not help at all.
No, I have not changed soaps or detergents, had no unusual food or chemical exposures, and have not traveled recently.
I dread taking showers now, and the burning sensation in my feet makes it difficult to fall asleep at night.
I figured I must have developed a harsh allergy to the minerals in our tap water and some kind of nerve circulation trouble in my toes.
I'm terrified this redness and burning are signs of lupus or another condition that will make it impossible for me to keep working.
I have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, lung disease, or any other chronic medical conditions.
I had my appendix removed about twenty-five years ago without complications, but no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I am not taking any prescription medications, just a daily multivitamin.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only have a glass of wine socially on weekends, perhaps once or twice a month.
I work full-time in an office as an accountant, and I live comfortably at home with my husband.
There is no family history of blood disorders, early strokes, or clotting problems; my parents only had high blood pressure in older age.
I went through menopause five years ago at age fifty-one and have had no vaginal bleeding or spotting since.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, pulse 78 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air.
Prominently plethoric, ruddy facial complexion noted; patient appears comfortable at rest with excoriations from scratching.
Bilateral conjunctival injection present without conjunctival pallor or scleral icterus.
Linear excoriations on trunk and extremities without primary rash or hives; bilateral toes show notable erythema and warmth.
Normal vesicular breath sounds heard symmetrically throughout both lung fields without wheezes or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2 heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops appreciated.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no visible distension, collateral veins, or surgical scars.
Abdomen is soft and completely non-tender throughout with no muscular guarding or rebound tenderness.
Firm, smooth spleen tip is palpable 3 to 4 cm below the left costal margin; liver edge is not palpable below right costal margin.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are brisk, symmetric, and 2+ bilaterally.
No pretibial pitting edema bilaterally; toes are warm and flushed with rapid capillary refill under two seconds.
Motor strength is 5/5 across all major muscle groups in both upper and lower extremities.
